RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Amina Adebayo lives in a rented room in Mushin, Lagos. She works as a day laborer sweeping rubble at a building site, earning 500 naira for the day, with no guaranteed work tomorrow. In the afternoon she attends a vocational carpentry course, where she is the only woman; she sits near the back and watches the instructor's hands, waiting to ask rehearsed questions. She keeps a worn notebook recording expenses (50 naira for water, 100 for groundnuts, 200 for a notebook leaf) in school-learned English. Her tools—a hammer, a chisel, a small saw—are stored in a locked metal box under her bed; she oils the hinges every Friday evening, a ritual taught by her late father before he died of a fever when she was twelve. Since then she has learned to depend on order: double-checking measurements before cutting, measuring again afterwards, triple-checking the lock, and counting each day's coins. She values caution, order, and self-reliance; she treats caution as the only wealth she has ever reliably owned. She values thrift as necessity; she accounts every expense against rent, food, or lessons. She wants to be generous but experiences giving as a loss against an uncertain future; she secretly slips an extra piece of maize to a neighbor's child. She holds a quiet, tight faith and prays in the morning not for riches but for no accident on the site, no broken tool, no sudden illness. She believes school-learned English and training can open doors. She speaks Yoruba with her landlady and Pidgin at the site, but writes in careful, school-learned English. She does not laugh easily, but smiles to herself when Emeka, a quiet older trainee, taps his foot in rhythm. Her mother lives in Ibadan and sends notes only for urgent family events; she expects Amina to maintain ties despite distance. Her aunt is her mother's elder sister, values large family gatherings, and will notice Amina's absence. Emeka sometimes shares his offcuts with her and has become a silent ally in the workshop. When faced with competing obligations, Amina previously skipped a family wedding to attend an extra carpentry session, then sent a small gift later. She regularly postpones minor purchases, such as replacing a worn sandal, to keep her tool fund intact. She is a vocational carpentry trainee and a day laborer; she rents a room and manages income for rent, food, and lessons. She maintains the Friday-evening ritual of oiling her tool box hinges. She is the daughter of her mother in Ibadan and niece of her mother's elder sister. Her income is tightly allocated; tool repair or replacement is a strain; her afternoon course restricts availability. She reads and writes English and speaks Yoruba and Pidgin.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

After her morning sweep, Amina's landlady stops her in the courtyard and hands her a folded note from Amina's mother. The note announces that her cousin's baby will be named next Saturday in Ibadan and her aunt expects her to attend. The ceremony will last all day; Amina would need to miss her carpentry class and pay for transport. Her mother writes that she can borrow a lace blouse from her sister. Amina has only a few days to reply. Her tools need oil that weekend, and she cannot afford both the trip and a new chisel. She stands by the gate holding the note.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

She has just finished sweeping rubble and is breathing heavily; the morning heat already beads sweat on her forehead. Her hands are calloused and slightly sore from gripping the broom handle. She is hungry, having eaten only a piece of leftover garri before dawn. The note's handwriting—her mother's rounded letters—reminds her of the day her father died, when her mother wrote the same careful script to tell the school she would not return. The phrase 'naming ceremony' recalls her own first day at the carpentry class, when she introduced herself and no one replied.
